title: Systematic review of research on artificial intelligence applications in higher education – where are the educators?
venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
extended_summary:
This paper asks how artificial intelligence (AI) has been studied and applied in higher education, where the research is coming from, and whether authors critically discuss ethical challenges and risks. Rather than testing a single intervention, it systematically reviews peer-reviewed journal articles published from 2007 to November 2018 and synthesizes the scope of AI uses in higher education.

The review screened 2,656 records and included 146 articles. The paper organizes AI applications into four main areas: profiling and prediction, intelligent tutoring systems, assessment and evaluation, and adaptive systems/personalisation. The studies span both student-facing and institution-facing uses, such as dropout prediction, automated grading, feedback systems, adaptive learning environments, and tutoring systems. Most studies were quantitative and drawn heavily from computer science and STEM fields; only a small minority came from education departments.

The population focus was predominantly undergraduate students, with a smaller number of postgraduate studies. The context was higher education institutions across many countries, with the largest share of studies coming from the United States, China, Taiwan, and Turkey. The review concludes that AI research in higher education is expanding, but the literature shows limited explicit definitions of AI, very little critical reflection on privacy, ethics, and cost, and a weak connection to pedagogical theory. It calls for more educator involvement and more attention to ethical and educational perspectives.

identified_tools.name: ITS (General)
identified_tools.description: Intelligent tutoring systems are AI-based educational systems that simulate aspects of one-to-one tutoring by adapting instruction, providing hints or feedback, diagnosing learner needs, and sometimes supporting collaboration or teacher workflows.
identified_tools.use_case: This paper is a systematic review of higher-education AI research; ITS is one of the four main application categories synthesized from the included studies, with subtypes such as teaching content, automated feedback, curating materials, and facilitating collaboration.

findings.finding_summary: Across the 29 ITS studies included in the review, most implementations reported positive or satisfactory preliminary results, though the authors note that these were typically short-term studies and did not account for novelty effects. The review also cites an earlier meta-analysis of 39 ITS studies by Steenbergen-Hu and Cooper (2014), which found a moderate effect on learning, that ITS were less effective than human tutoring, but outperformed traditional classroom instruction, reading printed or digital text, or homework assignments.
findings.measure: Review synthesis of ITS study outcomes; prior meta-analysis of learning outcomes
findings.effect_size: moderate effect (meta-analysis cited in review); exact pooled effect size not reported in this paper
findings.sample_size: n=29 ITS studies in this review; meta-analysis of n=39 studies cited

quality_tier_rationale: This is a systematic review, but it synthesizes heterogeneous ITS studies rather than evaluating a single intervention with experimental controls. The paper also reports limited critical appraisal and mostly short-term evidence.
impact_tier_rationale: The review reports generally positive preliminary effects for ITS and cites a moderate meta-analytic impact, but exact effect sizes are not provided in this paper and the evidence is indirect for any single tool. The overall impact therefore appears modest to unclear at the review level.
